records.name: AgentBench
records.short_description: A multi-environment benchmark for LLM agents across OS, database, knowledge-graph, game, shopping, household, and web tasks.
records.status_evidence: Superseded by AgentBench FC (2025-10-10, 5-env function-calling containerized protocol via AgentRL). Original 8-env remains discriminative at ~31% OA but main branch now serves FC; v0.1/v0.2 are archived and new evaluations should use FC (see github.com/THUDM/AgentBench — 'revert to v0.1/v0.2' for original).

paper.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents

metric.primary: overall AgentBench score (%) — weighted average of 8 environments
metric.aggregation: OA from Table 3 is out of 10 (max 10); this site normalizes to percent (OA×10) for chart parity with FC and other benchmarks. Weighted by 1/avg-task-score (Table 2 Weight-1). Report AgentBench version, split, task set, model, scaffold, and prompts

variants.name: AgentBench FC
variants.description: Function-calling prompt version integrated with AgentRL and containerized deployment for ALFWorld, DBBench, Knowledge Graph, OS interaction, and WebShop.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: varies substantially by task environment, interaction cap, retry policy, and whether the function-calling or original protocol is used

human_baseline.note: The benchmark is built from human-solvable interactive tasks, but no single blind human aggregate score is protocol-comparable across all eight original environments.

records.statistical_note: AgentBench scores are system scores, not model-only scores. Task server implementation, context management, retries, tool wrappers, and split choice can change the result.

contamination.mitigation: The original dev split is public while the official test split is not fully exposed. AgentBench FC improves deployment reproducibility, but public code and environment descriptions still create scaffold overfitting risk.

changelog.note: Set status to deprecated with successor agentbench-fc: original 8-env superseded by FC (2025-10-10), main branch now FC, v0.1/v0.2 archived; timeline stays OA-only (OA×10 → %) per arXiv:2308.03688v3.
Normalize Table 3 OA scores to percent (OA×10, max 10→100%) per arXiv:2308.03688v3; source pinned to v3. Timeline remains original 8-env series only with successor agentbench-fc.
Restrict timeline to original AgentBench 8-env series only (remove FC points per owner request); set successor to agentbench-fc and clarify FC is not plotted on same axis.
Added performance timeline points using AgentBench OA scores from Table 3 and model launch dates no earlier than the benchmark release.
Initial page. Treats the 2023/ICLR 2024 AgentBench benchmark as the main lineage and notes the 2025 AgentBench FC update without mixing FC and original scores.

records.name: AgentIF
records.short_description: 707 instructions from 50 real-world agents, averaging 1,723 words and 11.9 constraints — whether instruction following survives deployment-scale prompts.
records.status_evidence: Moved to the site's nearing-saturation bucket: the benchmark is still useful for exposing agentic constraint failures, but the public static set is small, top CSR is already near 60%, and the main value is shifting from broad frontier ranking to targeted failure analysis.

paper.title: AgentIF: Benchmarking Instruction Following of Large Language Models in Agentic Scenarios

authors.name: Bin Xu
authors.affiliation: Tsinghua University / Beijing Academy of AI

metric.judge_model: Evaluator LLM (paper uses GPT-4o / gpt-4o-2024-11-20 for the LLM-based and hybrid constraint checks; some constraints use pure code verification, so not every item passes through the judge)
metric.aggregation: CSR averages the pass rate over all annotated constraints; ISR is the fraction of instructions where every constraint is met (an AND across constraints)

variants.name: ISR
variants.description: Instruction Success Rate — the proportion of instructions in which all constraints are simultaneously satisfied. The report's headline (best model ~27%).

variants.name: CSR
variants.description: Constraint Success Rate — the proportion of individual constraints correctly satisfied, averaged across all constraints and instructions.

human_baseline.note: No protocol-comparable aggregate human baseline is reported. Annotations were by humans, so ISR at full annotation agreement is implicit; the paper does not publish a 'human would score X' figure.

records.statistical_note: 707 instructions → an ISR near 27% has a rough 95% binomial interval of about ±3 points; constraints are nested inside instructions, so treating items as independent understates the variance.

contamination.mitigation: The prompts are drawn from real deployed agents and open-source workflows and are public on HuggingFace since release; nothing is held out or refreshed. Note the instructions themselves are real system prompts, so a model may have already seen structurally similar living workflows in pretraining — but the specific query/constraint pairings are bespoke.

changelog.note: Changed status from active to nearing-saturation per site taxonomy update; saturated_date remains null because the page is not marked saturated.
Cleared the paper venue to null: the arXiv record for AgentIF (2505.16944) carries no peer-reviewed venue at time of writing, so a claimed 'NeurIPS 2025' was unsourceable and removed.

Initial page. Timeline is sparse and only carries sourced points from the paper's Table 2 CSR values (o1-mini 59.8, GPT-4o 58.5) on the CSR axis; ISR is lower (~27%) and is documented in prose rather than mixed onto the timeline to keep the axis uniform. License not published for the dataset, so `license` is set to the paper/repo URL rather than a license identifier (gap noted).

records.name: AGIEval
records.short_description: Standardized human exams — SATs, LSATs, China's Gaokao and civil-service tests — repurposed to grade models against real human test-takers.
records.status_evidence: GPT-4 already cleared the average-human line (67%) on several sections at launch; by 2024 frontier models pushed the 20-task aggregate past the average human and near the top-percentile 91% ceiling, and the human-exam framing lost its discriminative power at the top. saturated_date (2024-06) marks the GPT-4-class era where the average-human baseline stopped separating strong models.

paper.title: AGIEval: A Human-Centric Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models

metric.aggregation: unweighted (macro) average across the 20 tasks — each exam section counts equally regardless of its question count; the headline setting is zero-shot with chain-of-thought

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 5–20 (8,062 exam questions; zero-shot CoT traces on multi-step problems dominate token cost)

human_baseline.note: Average human test-taker across the exam sections (~67%). The paper also reports a top-percentile ceiling of ~91% (top 1% of candidates, except the lawyer qualification test's top 10%). The gauge/timeline use the average-human figure as the reference line; the 91% top-human ceiling is the harder target the paper highlights. Both are MEASURED from real exam-taker distributions, not estimated — a key differentiator of AGIEval.

records.statistical_note: 8,062 questions across 20 unequally-sized exam sections; because the aggregate is an unweighted task average, a small section (e.g. a few hundred cloze items) moves the headline as much as a large one. Per-section scores — not the 20-task mean — are where the remaining signal lives now that the aggregate is saturated.

contamination.mitigation: None built in. AGIEval is drawn from real, published exams (SAT, LSAT, Gaokao, Chinese civil-service and bar exams), so the exact questions and worked solutions circulate widely on test-prep sites and in web-scale training data. There is no held-out or refreshed variant, and exam questions are exactly the kind of high-value content trainers scrape. Treat post-2023 scores as memorization-inclusive.

changelog.note: Initial page. First bilingual entry (english + chinese). Timeline holds the three launch-era points from the paper (text-davinci-003 37.4, ChatGPT 43.2, GPT-4 58.4) on the zero-shot-CoT 20-task macro-average axis, marked independent (the authors evaluated models they did not build), source arXiv:2304.06364. Later frontier scores (near the 91% top-human ceiling) are described in prose but NOT plotted: no cleanly-sourced, metric-consistent modern aggregate on the same all-20-task zero-shot-CoT axis was found, so points were omitted rather than fabricated. Human baseline stored as the measured average (67); the top-percentile 91% ceiling is recorded in the note. Schema note: `human_baseline` holds a single score — for AGIEval the average-human is the line and the top-human ceiling lives in the note; see the summary flag on whether the schema should eventually carry multiple baselines.

Expanded performance timeline with GPT-4o (few-shot), Qwen2.5 72B (base 0-shot), and DeepSeek-V3 (base 0-shot) scores. These use different eval settings (few-shot or 0-shot no-CoT) from the original paper's zero-shot-CoT axis, so they are marked with protocol notes and not directly comparable to the original three points.

records.name: AIME
records.short_description: The MAA's competition exam — 15 integer-answer problems per test, refreshed yearly so each new exam is briefly contamination-free.
records.status_evidence: AIME's status is genuinely split by its yearly refresh. OLD exams are saturated and contaminated: reasoning models solved AIME 2024 (o3 ~96.7%, up from GPT-4o's 13.4%). Each FRESH exam has a shrinking clean window, but frontier models now score high even on fresh exams (AIME 2025 ~85–91%). So the rolling benchmark is nearing-saturation — no single exam discriminates for long, yet the yearly refresh keeps briefly-clean signal alive. The plotted gauge/timeline is the AIME 2024 progression (one exam); the perpetual benchmark's yearly reset is described in prose, since the signature gauge shows one monotonic climb and cannot depict a reset.

authors.name: Mathematical Association of America (MAA)
authors.affiliation: competition organizer — AIME is an exam, not a research dataset; no paper

records.maintainer: Mathematical Association of America (MAA), administering AIME since 1983; problems compiled and evaluated by the community (MathArena, per-year HuggingFace sets)

metric.primary: accuracy — every answer is an integer 000–999, exact match (%)
metric.aggregation: mean over an exam's 15 questions (or a year's 30, both exams); because N is tiny, headline numbers are pass@1 AVERAGED over many samples (avg@k) or majority-voted (maj@64) — see Scoring methodology

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 1–10 per exam-year, but heavily sampling-dependent: because headline numbers use avg@k or maj@64, the real cost is k× a single pass — running maj@64 on a reasoning model is dozens of long chains per question

human_baseline.note: The line is the median AIME score, ~5 out of 15 (≈33%): 2024 AIME I had median 5 / mean 5.89, AIME II median 5 / mean 5.45. The crucial context, unlike MATH's 'which human' range: AIME takers are ALREADY an elite pool — the top ~5% of AMC qualifiers — and even they median only a third of the exam; a perfect 15/15 is achieved by only a few students per exam. So the baseline is LOW even for excellent humans, which is exactly what made frontier models scoring 90%+ so striking. (Note: the gauge shades 'above baseline' as its saturation zone; for AIME that region reads as 'above the median qualifier', not 'near the 100% ceiling' — the true ceiling is a perfect score, which top humans do reach.)

records.statistical_note: This is the sharpest sample-size trap on the wiki. One AIME exam is 15 questions, so ONE question = 6.7 points; a full year (30 questions, both exams) is 3.3 points per question. A 'model A beats model B by one question' gap is essentially noise — which is the entire reason labs run heavy sampling (avg@k / maj@64) instead of a single pass. Never trust a small AIME gap, and never compare a single-sample number against an avg@64 one.

contamination.mitigation: AIME is the wiki's first benchmark where REFRESH is the contamination defense — the concrete illustration of the yearly-refresh strategy the GSM8K and MATH pages point toward. Each new exam is genuinely unseen at release (a real, brand-new competition), giving a brief clean measurement window. But within months the problems and worked solutions flood the web, so that year's exam becomes contaminated: AIME 2024 is now high-contamination, while a current-year exam is briefly clean. The defense is rolling, not permanent — which is why risk is 'medium' (fresh yearly, decays fast), not low (no exam stays clean) or high (there is always a fresh, uncontaminated exam to run).

changelog.note: Initial page. Third `maths` benchmark (after GSM8K, MATH). Two firsts: no research paper (paper: null — schema made `paper` nullable this commit, with FactsSidebar guarding the paper row) and a refresh_cycle where the refresh IS the point (yearly). launch_date 2024-02-01 = AIME 2024 / the modern LLM-benchmark era; the exam itself has run since 1983 (Overview) — same precedent as AGIEval dating to its benchmark use, not its source material. Timeline is a SINGLE exam (AIME 2024), pass@1: GPT-4o 13.4 → o1 74.4 → o3 96.7 (all vendor-reported, OpenAI posts). Fresh-year exams (AIME 2025 ~85–91%: Grok 4 90.6, o3-mini 86.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro 85.8; AIME 2026 on MathArena) are DELIBERATELY not plotted — different tests, mixing exam-years on one axis is a comparability trap. Human baseline 33 (median ~5/15 among already-elite qualifiers). status nearing-saturation (rolling-window reasoning documented). SCHEMA FLAGS in summary: (a) timeline points want structured exam_year + sampling fields; (b) pass_at can't express avg@k/maj@64; (c) gauge can't depict a yearly reset.

records.name: ARC-AGI
records.short_description: Colored-grid abstraction tasks that test few-shot rule induction, not memorized facts, language fluency, or school math.
records.status_evidence: ARC-AGI-1 remains useful as a historical abstraction benchmark, but the official ARC Prize leaderboard generated on 2026-07-23 lists multiple verified systems above 95% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private axis, including GPT-5.6 Sol at 97.5%. ARC Prize launched ARC-AGI-2 because ARC-AGI-1 had become too brute-forceable and less discriminative for frontier systems.

paper.title: On the Measure of Intelligence

metric.primary: task success rate on the evaluation split (%)
metric.aggregation: percentage of evaluation tasks solved; a task is solved only when every predicted output grid exactly matches the target grid, including dimensions and every cell

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: varies by test-time reasoning budget; the official ARC Prize leaderboard reports modern semi-private ARC-AGI-1 runs from cents per task to several dollars per task, while older o3-preview high-compute reports were much more expensive

human_baseline.note: The official ARC Prize leaderboard lists a Human Panel score of 98% on the ARC-AGI-1 semi-private axis. Older public-page summaries also report lower average-human estimates; the sidebar uses the current official leaderboard value.

records.statistical_note: The public evaluation split has 400 tasks, but ARC Prize leaderboard scores use the semi-private axis and competitions may use private splits. Treat scores as comparable only when the split, attempt budget, model/system type, and cost budget are named.

contamination.mitigation: The public train and evaluation tasks are fully available on GitHub. ARC Prize later introduced semi-private and private evaluation sets for leaderboard and competition testing, but ARC-AGI-1 still has a fixed, old private pool and a long history of submissions. Contamination risk is therefore high for public-set scores and medium-to-high even for public leaderboard comparisons unless the split and testing policy are clear.

changelog.note: Updated with the official ARC Prize leaderboard data generated 2026-07-23: Human Panel 98%, Claude 4.7 High 93.5%, GPT-5.5 Pro High 96.5%, and GPT-5.6 Sol xHigh 97.5% on ARC-AGI-1 semi-private. Historical o3-preview context was retained.

Initial page. Timeline uses official ARC Prize / ARC-AGI-Pub points only: GPT-4o 5%, o1-preview 18%, Jeremy Berman 53.6%, and o3-preview-low 75.7% on the semi-private leaderboard axis. Public-eval and high-compute o3 numbers are discussed in prose but not mixed into the chart.

records.name: ARC-AGI-2
records.short_description: The harder static ARC successor: human-calibrated colored-grid abstraction tasks, now pressured by 2026 frontier systems.
records.status_evidence: ARC-AGI-2 remains the current static colored-grid ARC benchmark, but the official ARC Prize leaderboard generated on 2026-07-23 lists GPT-5.6 Sol Max at 92.5% and GPT-5.6 Sol xHigh at 90.0% on the ARC-AGI-2 semi-private axis. Because competition/private-set validation and efficiency constraints still matter, this page marks it nearing saturation rather than fully saturated.

paper.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems

metric.primary: task success rate on the public evaluation split (%)
metric.aggregation: percentage of evaluation tasks solved; a task is solved only when every predicted output grid exactly matches the target grid, with two output attempts allowed per test input

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: model- and search-budget-dependent; the official ARC Prize leaderboard generated 2026-07-23 lists semi-private ARC-AGI-2 runs from cents per task to more than $10/task, with GPT-5.6 Sol Max at $1.44/task

human_baseline.note: The official ARC Prize leaderboard lists a Human Panel score of 100% on the ARC-AGI-2 semi-private axis. The arXiv paper also reports 66% across all human evaluations and attempts, 75% aggregated by task, and 100% solvability by at least two independent non-expert human testers.

records.statistical_note: The public evaluation set has 120 tasks, so one solved task moves the score by 0.83 points. The official leaderboard uses the semi-private axis, while Kaggle competitions use private evaluation. Identify the split, attempt budget, and cost budget before comparing scores.

contamination.mitigation: ARC-AGI-2 keeps public training and evaluation data for open research, but adds semi-private and fully-private test sets for lower-leakage leaderboard and competition use. The public evaluation split is still public, so repeated tuning against it should be treated as contamination.

changelog.note: Updated paper citation to arXiv:2505.11831v2 and added current official leaderboard points generated 2026-07-23. Status changed to nearing-saturation because the semi-private leaderboard now lists systems above the 85% target, while private competition validation remains a separate claim.

Initial page. Timeline uses the official ARC Prize launch table for ARC-AGI-2 only. Scores marked as estimates in the ARC Prize report are kept in the prose context and model labels rather than normalized into unsourced leaderboard history.

records.name: ARC-AGI-3
records.short_description: Interactive ARC environments that score agents by human-relative action efficiency, planning, exploration, and adaptation.
records.status_evidence: ARC-AGI-3 is newly introduced as an interactive reasoning benchmark. The paper reports that humans solved 100% of environments while frontier AI systems scored below 1% as of March 2026, and the official leaderboard generated on 2026-07-23 still shows low semi-private scores despite visible progress.

paper.title: ARC-AGI-3: A New Challenge for Frontier Agentic Intelligence

metric.primary: Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) on interactive environments (%)
metric.aggregation: per-level action efficiency relative to human baselines, normalized per environment and aggregated across environments; a 100% score means agents beat every game as efficiently as humans

variants.name: environment completion
variants.description: Whether the agent completes levels and environments under the configured action and time budgets.

variants.name: cost-normalized leaderboard view
variants.description: The official leaderboard plots performance against run cost because interactive exploration can spend very different amounts of compute.

run_config.shots: first exposure to each interactive environment

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: varies by agent and interaction budget; the official leaderboard generated 2026-07-23 lists semi-private ARC-AGI-3 runs from roughly $2.3k to more than $25k total

human_baseline.note: The ARC-AGI-3 paper and ARC Prize overview state that environments are 100% human-solvable; the score definition treats 100% as beating every game as efficiently as humans.

records.statistical_note: ARC-AGI-3 scores are not exact-match grid accuracies. They are human-relative efficiency scores over interactive environments. Public-demo, semi-private, and fully-private results should not be mixed without naming the split and budget.

contamination.mitigation: The 25 public demo environments are intentionally easier and do not comprehensively represent the private mechanics. The benchmark uses 55 semi-private and 55 fully-private environments as the main evaluation sets, with the fully private set reserved for tightly guarded competition use.

changelog.note: Initial page created from the ARC-AGI-3 overview, arXiv:2603.24621v2, and the official ARC Prize leaderboard data generated 2026-07-23. Timeline uses semi-private leaderboard points and converts source decimals to percentages.

records.name: AV-SpeakerBench
records.short_description: Speaker-centric audiovisual benchmark for aligning who speaks, what is said, and when in real multi-person videos.
records.status_evidence: A new 2025 benchmark with a 20.7-point gap between the paper's strongest model and human performance, plus large audio-versus-vision ablation gaps across 12 tasks.

paper.title: See, Hear, and Understand: Benchmarking Audiovisual Human Speech Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models

authors.name: Samuel Low Yu Hang et al.

records.license: MIT dataset metadata; source videos remain subject to their original terms

metric.aggregation: overall accuracy across 3,212 four-choice questions, with per-task reporting across 12 speaker-, visual-, and audio-centric task types

variants.name: audiovisual
variants.description: Canonical condition with synchronized audio and video.

variants.name: visual-only ablation
variants.description: Removes audio to measure how often visual cues alone support the answer.

variants.name: audio-only ablation
variants.description: Removes video to measure the contribution of visible identity and events.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: high for native audiovisual APIs; cost depends strongly on video duration and frame sampling density

human_baseline.note: Paper-reported human overall accuracy under the benchmark protocol.

records.statistical_note: Overall accuracy can hide fusion failures because task frequencies differ and some items remain inferable from natural visual speech cues. Report per-task results and visual-only/audio-only ablations alongside the audiovisual score.

contamination.mitigation: Expert curation, cross-modal question construction, temporal-sensitivity checks, and unimodal filtering reduce shortcuts at release; the public dataset can still enter later training corpora.

changelog.note: Initial page based on arXiv v2, the official project, and the official Hugging Face dataset.

records.name: BFCL / Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard
records.short_description: A live UC Berkeley leaderboard for function and tool calling across AST, executable, multi-turn, live, and agentic categories.
records.status_evidence: BFCL V4 is the current leaderboard series: the official site was last updated on 2026-04-12, evaluates agentic web-search and memory categories, and pins reproductions to bfcl-eval==2025.12.17 / commit f7cf735.

paper.title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models

metric.aggregation: BFCL V4 combines Agentic, Multi-Turn, Live, Non-Live, and Hallucination categories using fixed top-level weights; within many categories, subcategories are averaged independently of raw item count

variants.name: AST accuracy
variants.description: Parses predicted calls into abstract syntax trees and checks function name, argument structure, and values for non-live categories.

variants.name: Executable accuracy
variants.description: Runs live or executable calls where static AST equivalence is insufficient.

variants.name: Agentic web search and memory
variants.description: BFCL V4 categories that test multi-hop web search, error recovery, and read/write memory tool use.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: the official leaderboard reports estimated cost and latency; total cost depends on selected categories, native function calling versus prompt format, and model pricing

human_baseline.note: No single human baseline is published for the full BFCL V4 weighted score.

records.statistical_note: The V4 overall score is a weighted category composite, not a micro-average over every exposed row. Always report native function-calling versus prompt mode, selected categories, code commit, and bfcl-eval package version.

contamination.mitigation: BFCL adds live and periodically updated data, category expansion, reproducible pinned commits, and model-response releases, but the public test data still creates memorization and prompt-format overfitting risk.

changelog.note: Added BFCL V4 leaderboard graph points using model launch dates rather than leaderboard update dates.
Initial page. Uses BFCL V4 as the current score series and records the official V4 category composition instead of mixing older V1/V2/V3 results.

records.name: BIG-Bench
records.short_description: 204-task community-built mega-suite spanning reasoning, knowledge, math, code and social bias — the sprawling proving ground BBH was distilled from.
records.status_evidence: No longer maintained as an evaluation target. Its 'canary' GUID — meant to keep tasks out of training data — was widely ignored, so the suite leaked into web-scale corpora; task quality is famously uneven; and the field moved to distillates like BBH. Deprecated rather than saturated: models don't uniformly max it, it simply stopped being used.

paper.title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models

records.maintainer: Google & the BIG-bench collaboration (~450 authors across 132 institutions); repo google/BIG-bench

metric.aggregation: Each of the 204 tasks defines its own 'preferred metric' (multiple-choice grade, exact-match, BLEU/ROUGE, or a custom scorer); per-task scores are normalized (roughly 0 = poor, 100 = expert-rubric) and averaged. The aggregate is highly sensitive to which task subset is included and how tasks are weighted — see Known issues.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: Highly variable — the full 204-task suite is large and heterogeneous; most users run BIG-bench Lite (24 tasks) or single tasks rather than the whole thing

human_baseline.note: The paper collected per-task human-rater performance (average rater and best rater), but reports no single suite-wide aggregate human score we can cite here — human performance is only meaningful task by task.

records.statistical_note: A suite-level number hides enormous per-task variance: tasks range from a handful to thousands of examples, and from trivial to near-impossible. Never compare models on the BIG-Bench aggregate alone — the task mix and weighting dominate the headline figure.

contamination.mitigation: Every task file embeds a 'canary' GUID string that trainers are asked not to strip, so they can detect and exclude BIG-bench from crawled data. In practice the canary was widely ignored, and the suite leaked into training corpora anyway — the field's most-cited example of a decontamination mechanism that depends on voluntary compliance and therefore failed.

changelog.note: Initial page. No performance timeline: the suite's normalized aggregate mixes heterogeneous per-task metrics and there is no cleanly-sourced, metric-consistent model time series to plot — per-task scores are the meaningful unit, so the timeline is intentionally empty rather than fabricated. Schema extended this commit: added `secondary_capabilities[]` (this suite spans several) and a `composite` scoring value (no single scoring rule applies to a suite).

records.name: BIG-Bench Hard
records.short_description: 23 BIG-Bench tasks where models trailed humans — the benchmark that proved chain-of-thought prompting works, then fell to the reasoning-model era.
records.status_evidence: Frontier and reasoning-tuned models exceed ~90% on the 23-task average and are near-perfect on many individual tasks; the reasoning-model era made BBH trivial. Google DeepMind built BBEH (2025) — replacing each task with a harder counterpart — precisely because BBH stopped discriminating at the top.

paper.title: Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them

records.maintainer: Mirac Suzgun et al. (Google Research); repo suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard

metric.aggregation: unweighted (macro) average across the 23 tasks — each task counts equally regardless of how many examples it has

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 5–20 (6,511 items; 3-shot chain-of-thought prompts are long, and the reasoning traces dominate token cost)

human_baseline.note: Average human-rater performance across the 23 tasks in the original paper; the best (max) human rater averaged ~94.4%. BBH tasks were selected precisely as the BIG-Bench tasks where prior models fell below the 67.7% average-rater line. (Canonical Table 1 values from the paper.)

records.statistical_note: 6,511 examples across 23 unequally-sized tasks; because the aggregate is an unweighted task average, a small task moves the number as much as a large one. Now that the mean is saturated, per-task scores — not the 23-task average — are where any remaining signal lives.

contamination.mitigation: Inherits BIG-bench's public tasks and its widely-ignored canary GUID. BBH's popularity made it especially likely to appear in pretraining and instruction-tuning data, and there is no refreshed variant. Its high contamination risk is a direct reason BBEH was built with fresh tasks.

changelog.note: Initial page. Timeline holds the two canonical paper points — PaLM 540B and Codex code-davinci-002 with 3-shot chain-of-thought (arXiv:2210.09261), marked independent (the paper evaluated models it did not build).
Expanded performance timeline with GPT-4, Gemini Ultra, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and DeepSeek V3 scores. BBH is now saturated as documented in the prose.

records.name: BrowseComp
records.short_description: OpenAI's benchmark for browsing agents that must find hard-to-locate, short-answer facts on the web.
records.status_evidence: BrowseComp is nearing saturation: launch baseline Deep Research 51.5% (Apr 2025, openai.com/index/browsecomp); by Aug 2026 SOTA reached 92.2% (GPT-5.6 Sol) with top-3 within 1.4 pts (llm-stats.com/benchmarks/browsecomp, benchlm.ai) and only ~7.8 pts headroom. LoHoSearch reports 'rapidly saturated... surpassing 90%... 30%->90% in barely ten months' (arxiv.org/abs/2606.12837) and Anthropic shows eval-awareness/decrypted answer key (anthropic.com/engineering/eval-awareness-browsecomp); LiveBrowseComp confirms IKD leakage (arxiv.org/abs/2605.28721).

paper.title: BrowseComp: A Simple Yet Challenging Benchmark for Browsing Agents

records.license: MIT (simple-evals code); dataset terms follow the OpenAI simple-evals release

metric.aggregation: mean accuracy over short-answer browsing questions; predictions are compared against reference answers with the official simple-evals BrowseComp evaluator

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: can be high for deep browsing agents because many questions require long searches across many sites; report search/tool budget and retry policy

human_baseline.note: OpenAI's verification campaign reports trainers solved 29.2% of 1,255 checked problems within the allowed search process; among solved problems, trainer and reference answers matched 86.4%.

records.statistical_note: BrowseComp uses short answers to simplify grading. Scores depend strongly on browser/search tool quality, time budget, and whether the agent is allowed repeated attempts or parallel search.

records.name: ComplexBench
records.short_description: Bilingual benchmark of how models follow instructions when several constraints must hold at once — where stacking constraints is not linear.

paper.title: ComplexBench: Benchmarking Complex Instruction-Following with Multiple Constraints Composition

metric.judge_model: GPT-4, augmented with rule-based checks where a constraint is verifiable programmatically (e.g. length), per the paper's evaluation protocol

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: Judge-pass dominates: every generated response is re-read by the GPT-4 evaluator per scoring question, so cost scales with dataset size and the number of constraint checks. A small run on the released subset is inexpensive; a full pass is non-trivial.

human_baseline.note: No protocol-comparable human constraint-satisfaction baseline was published. The dataset is manually curated and validated by humans, but the authors do not report a human pass-rate that maps one-to-one onto the automatic judge score.

records.statistical_note: The overall percentage is a composite built over per-instance dependency trees, not a clean binomial hit-rate, so simple confidence intervals mislead. Because many scoring questions gate on prerequisites, one early failure can cascade and suppress several downstream points at once.

contamination.mitigation: Items are largely self-contained synthetic compositions written for the benchmark rather than scraped from the internet, so the highest-risk web-memorization leak path is limited. records.name: FrontierMath
records.short_description: Original, unpublished research-level math problems by expert mathematicians — mostly private to resist contamination. Frontier models solved under 2% at launch.
records.status_evidence: The strongest active case on the wiki. At launch (Nov 2024) state-of-the-art models solved UNDER 2% — a benchmark frontier systems almost entirely fail. Reasoning models with Python tools have since climbed (OpenAI announced o3 at 25.2% in Dec 2024, tools-on), but that figure is contested — Epoch's own independent reproductions of comparable models came in far lower (~11%). By the June 2026 v2 release Epoch added a harder Tier 4 precisely because Tiers 1–3 progress had become significant, yet the hardest tier remains far from solved. Current figures move fast and are tool/compute-dependent — consult Epoch's live dashboard; this page does not restate unverified third-party numbers. Saturation here would mean research-level, closed-form mathematics is largely automated.

paper.title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI

authors.name: + a large collaborating group of research mathematicians

records.maintainer: Epoch AI (Glazer et al.), with problems authored by expert mathematicians; evaluations run by Epoch on the private set
records.license: proprietary (Epoch AI — private held-out set; a small set of sample problems is public)

metric.primary: accuracy — % of problems solved, automated answer verification (%)
metric.aggregation: per-tier accuracy on the PRIVATE set; answers are numerical / SymPy-checkable, so grading is automated equivalence, not human-judged. Reported per tier, not as one blended number

harnesses.name: Epoch AI (canonical — runs the private eval)

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: High and highly variable: problems take specialists hours to days, so models emit very long agentic traces with Python execution; heavy-compute / high-sample runs (which drive the highest reported numbers) cost far more than a single pass

human_baseline.note: No aggregate human baseline exists, and — as with HLE — none is well-defined in principle, only more so. These are research-level problems spanning many advanced fields; no single mathematician can solve across all of them. The meaningful human reference is per-problem: an expert in the relevant subfield solves it over hours to days. Fields Medalists who reviewed the problems underscored the point — Terence Tao said that in the near term 'the only way to solve them, short of having a real domain expert in the area, is to get a lucky overfit,' and predicted the hardest tier would 'resist AIs for several years.'

records.statistical_note: Scores are reported per tier, and the tiers are small (Tier 4 is 43 problems), so per-tier figures carry wide confidence intervals — a few problems move the percentage several points. Two deeper caveats dominate any FrontierMath number: (1) tools-on vs tools-off and heavy-compute vs single-pass swing results enormously (see Scoring methodology); (2) the set is private, so you are trusting Epoch's evaluation rather than reproducing it yourself. Always cite the tier, the tool/compute setting, and that it is an Epoch-run private-set number.

contamination.mitigation: The strongest contamination defense catalogued on the wiki — and the counter-model to AIME's yearly refresh and MMLU's fully-public exposure. The problems are ORIGINAL and UNPUBLISHED, and the benchmark is mostly PRIVATE by design: only a small sample set is public, and Epoch runs evaluations on a held-out set that is not released. The tradeoff is a different threat model: you cannot independently reproduce a private benchmark, so you must trust the evaluator (see Known issues). The privacy is also entangled with the funding history — OpenAI, which funded the dataset, had access to most problems, so Epoch established held-out sets the funder cannot see (53 solutions withheld in one version; 20 of 50 Tier 4 problems reserved) as a post-hoc safeguard.

performance_timeline.model: o3-mini high (Epoch independent eval, Tiers 1–3, tools-on)

changelog.note: Initial page. Fourth `maths` benchmark and the TOP of the GSM8K → MATH → AIME → FrontierMath headroom chain. Two firsts: first `public_test_set: false` (private held-out) and first `contamination.risk: low`. Sourcing was verified against Epoch AI and primary sources throughout; NO figures were taken from recollection or third-party aggregators. Timeline plots only Epoch-attributable numbers: launch best-frontier <2% (Epoch paper, arXiv:2411.04872) and Epoch's independent o3-mini-high eval ~11% (tools-on) — deliberately NOT OpenAI's announced 25.2%, which Epoch could not reproduce at that level (documented in Known issues). 2025–26 aggregator figures (reported in the 50–85% range for tools-on Tiers 1–3) were OMITTED as unverifiable against Epoch and given FrontierMath's inflation history. v2 (2026-06-12) expanded to 338 problems (Tiers 1–3: 295, Tier 4: 43). Funding-disclosure controversy documented neutrally in Known issues, cited to Epoch's own statement and TechCrunch. records.name: GPQA
records.short_description: PhD-written science questions so hard that skilled non-experts with Google score 34% — the 'Google-proof' exam, reported on its 198-question Diamond subset.
records.status_evidence: Frontier reasoning models reach the high 80s on GPQA Diamond (e.g. Grok 4 ~87%, mid-2025), against a label-noise-adjusted ceiling likely in the low 90s — the paper documents a few percent of questions with expert-identified errors. Unlike MMLU, meaningful headroom remains and top models are only now crossing the PhD-expert line, so it still discriminates; but the trajectory is one or two model generations from done. Judgment call — the first `nearing-saturation` benchmark on the wiki.

paper.title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark

records.maintainer: David Rein et al. (NYU, with Cohere and Anthropic-affiliated co-authors); repo github.com/idavidrein/gpqa

metric.primary: accuracy on GPQA Diamond, 4-option multiple choice (%)
metric.aggregation: mean accuracy over the 198 Diamond questions (the primary reported configuration; see the note on dataset.size)

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 2–15 on Diamond (198 items; reasoning-era models emit long chains of thought per question, which dominate token cost). The 448-question main or 546-question extended sets scale up proportionally.

human_baseline.note: PhD-domain experts scored 81.3% on the Diamond subset (the primary configuration this page reports); non-expert validators with unrestricted web access scored only 22.1% on Diamond. On the full 448-question main set the headline figures are ~65% expert (74% after discounting mistakes the experts themselves flagged in retrospect) and ~34% non-expert. IMPORTANT nuance: OpenAI, evaluating o1, recruited its own PhD experts who scored only 69.7% on Diamond — so whether a model 'beats PhD experts' depends entirely on which expert pool you compare against. The gauge/timeline use the paper's 81.3% Diamond expert accuracy as the reference line, because GPQA's entire claim is expert-level difficulty; beating the 22–34% non-expert line is trivial and not the point.

records.statistical_note: GPQA Diamond is only 198 questions. At ~80% accuracy that is a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±5.6 points (±7 near 50%). This is the single most important number on the page: a great many publicized 'Model A beats Model B by 2 points on GPQA Diamond' claims are statistically indistinguishable from noise. Treat any Diamond gap under ~6 points as unresolved, and prefer the larger main/extended sets when a comparison actually needs to be settled.

contamination.mitigation: The dataset is public but gated: HuggingFace access requires accepting an agreement, and the authors ask users NOT to post questions or answers online 'to reduce the risk of leakage into foundation model training corpora.' This is a voluntary pledge, not a technical control — the same class of opt-in decontamination that failed for BIG-Bench's canary. The set is fully static with no refreshed variant, and Diamond questions have been discussed and reproduced online since 2023, which pushes the effective risk from medium toward high over time.

changelog.note: Initial page. First `nearing-saturation` status on the wiki. Timeline is on the GPQA Diamond axis (the primary reported configuration): GPT-4o 56.1 and o1 78.0 (vendor-reported, OpenAI o1 post) and Grok 4 87.0 (independent, Epoch AI). GPT-4's ~39% launch baseline is the paper's strongest baseline on the MAIN set, not Diamond, so it is described in prose but NOT plotted — mixing subsets on one axis would be dishonest, and no cleanly-sourced GPT-4 Diamond launch point was found. 2025–26 scores in the low-to-mid 90s are discussed in prose but not plotted (no single authoritative source verified per model). Human baseline stored as the paper's 81.3% Diamond expert accuracy; the main-set 65%/74% figures, the 22.1%/34% non-expert figures, and OpenAI's 69.7% recruited-expert figure are all in the note. dataset.size is 198 (Diamond) per the size-matches-primary-configuration convention documented in Task details.

records.name: GSM8K
records.short_description: 8.5K grade-school math word problems (2–8 arithmetic steps) — the default elementary-math benchmark and the classic chain-of-thought demonstration.
records.status_evidence: Frontier models cleared ~95% by 2023–24 and the reasoning-model era pushed scores to ~97–99%, collapsing headroom. But saturation here is the sharpest 'saturated ≠ solved' case on the wiki: GSM-Symbolic (Apple, 2024) showed that changing only names/numbers, and especially adding one irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp), drops accuracy heavily across models — so the SCORE is saturated while the CAPABILITY (robust arithmetic reasoning) is not. saturated_date 2024-01 marks the point frontier scores stopped discriminating; the discriminating signal moved to harder math (MATH → AIME → FrontierMath) and to robustness variants.

paper.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems

records.maintainer: OpenAI (Cobbe et al.); repo openai/grade-school-math, dataset openai/gsm8k

metric.primary: accuracy — exact match on the final numeric answer (%)
metric.aggregation: mean over the 1,319 test problems; the answer after the '####' delimiter is compared, reasoning steps are not graded

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 1–5 (1,319 short test problems; chain-of-thought traces are modest. maj@k voting, which some headline numbers use, multiplies cost by k)

human_baseline.note: No measured human baseline. The paper states only an informal difficulty target: 'a bright middle school student should be able to solve every problem.' Because the problems are grade-school and were verified solvable, the implicit human ceiling is near 100% for a capable solver — but no human solve-rate was measured, so the score is null. Treat this like MMLU's estimated-baseline situation, only softer: a target description, not a number.

records.statistical_note: 1,319 test problems → ±~1.2pt (95% CI) near 95%, so at the saturated frontier ordinary model gaps are within noise. But the dominant caveat here is NOT sampling error — it is robustness: GSM-Symbolic shows the same model's accuracy swings by tens of points under trivial rewordings, so a single GSM8K number overstates reasoning reliability far more than its CI suggests. Also non-comparable across protocols (direct vs CoT vs maj@k).

contamination.mitigation: None. Public since 2021, MIT-licensed, and mirrored across the web WITH worked natural-language solutions — ideal memorization fodder. Fully static, no refresh. Structurally the same exposure that undid MMLU, and a direct reason the GSM-Symbolic and GSM8K-Platinum variants exist: to test whether a score survives when the exact public items are perturbed or cleaned.

changelog.note: Initial page. First `maths` capability on the wiki. Timeline traces the canonical chain-of-thought arc on GSM8K accuracy: GPT-3 175B fine-tuned ~35% (paper Fig 5 baseline, vendor-reported, arXiv:2110.14168), PaLM 540B 8-shot CoT 56.9% (Wei et al., arXiv:2201.11903, independent), PaLM 540B CoT+self-consistency 74.4% (Wang et al., arXiv:2203.11171, independent), GPT-4 5-shot CoT 92.0% (GPT-4 report, arXiv:2303.08774, vendor-reported). records.name: Humanity's Last Exam
records.short_description: ~2,500 expert-written questions across 100+ subjects, each filtered to stump frontier models — designed to be the final closed-ended academic benchmark.
records.status_evidence: The clearest active benchmark on the wiki. Launch scores were single digits (GPT-4o 3.3%, o1 9.1%, DeepSeek-R1 9.4%, no tools); the current no-tools frontier is ~38% (Gemini 3 Pro, Nov 2025) — a steep climb but a long way from solved. Given the 'last exam' thesis, saturation here would mean closed-ended academic testing has run out of headroom entirely, so 'what replaces it' points toward open-ended, agentic, and interactive evaluation rather than a harder Q&A set. Note: tool-augmented and agent scores run much higher and are tracked separately (see Timeline).

metric.judge_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, structured decoding) checks whether a model's answer is equivalent to the reference for the 80% short-answer questions. Judge model/version drift makes scores across grader versions not strictly comparable — pin the grader.
metric.aggregation: mean accuracy over ~2,500 questions; the headline configuration is closed-book (no tools, no browsing)

variants.name: RMS calibration error
variants.description: A second headline number, derived from the same graded correctness plus each answer's stated confidence: the root-mean-square gap between confidence and correctness (implementation from Hendrycks et al.). Launch models were ~80–93% — i.e. highly confident while almost always wrong. Not a separate grading protocol but a distinct measurement of overconfidence; reported alongside accuracy, never instead of it.
variants.judge_model: same GPT-4o judge (correctness component); confidence is model-reported

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 10–50 no-tools (~2,500 hard questions elicit long reasoning traces, plus a GPT-4o judge call each). Tool-augmented / agentic runs cost far more — browsing and multi-step search can multiply token use by 10x or more.

human_baseline.note: No human baseline — and here the concept itself breaks down. HLE spans 100+ expert subjects from classics to rocket engineering; no single human could sit the whole exam, so an aggregate 'human score' is undefined in principle, not merely unmeasured. This differs from SimpleQA, where a human COULD take the test but the score would mostly measure Googling: HLE is superhuman in BREADTH by construction. The only meaningful human reference is per-question — each was solved by the domain expert who wrote it — which is exactly why the benchmark exists: to test whether one model can match the union of many human specialists.

records.statistical_note: ~2,500 questions give a workable aggregate CI (±~2pt at 40%), but two non-sampling caveats dominate. First, scores move FAST — a published number is often stale within months (single digits to ~38% in under a year), so always read HLE figures with their date and this page's last_updated. Second, the number is meaningless without its CONFIGURATION: no-tools vs tool-augmented vs multi-agent 'heavy' modes differ by tens of points on the same model (see Timeline). Read accuracy beside calibration error, and never compare across tool settings.

contamination.mitigation: The strongest mitigation design catalogued on the wiki so far: alongside the public ~2,500-question set, CAIS/Scale hold a PRIVATE set of questions used to detect benchmark-specific overfitting by comparing a model's public vs private performance — a static-but-audited design. The public set is gated on HuggingFace (accept an agreement; users are asked not to re-share or re-upload). This does not make it leak-proof — the public questions are discussed online and the failure-filter selected for 2024-frontier blind spots — but the private audit catches the crudest gaming, which is why the risk is medium rather than high despite a fully static public set.

records.name: MATH
records.short_description: 12,500 AMC/AIME-level competition problems with worked solutions — usually evaluated on its 500-problem MATH-500 subset, the reasoning-model math standard.
records.status_evidence: MATH resisted far longer than GSM8K: GPT-4 managed only ~42% on the full set in 2023. But the reasoning-model era ended it — o1 (2024) reached ~94.8% on MATH-500 and later models sit in the 90s, so it no longer discriminates at the frontier. saturated_date 2024-09 marks the o1 inflection. As with GSM8K, saturated ≠ solved: exact-answer scoring hides whether the reasoning was valid, and headroom has moved to AIME and FrontierMath.

records.maintainer: Dan Hendrycks et al. (UC Berkeley); dataset hendrycks/competition_math. MATH-500 subset & PRM800K: OpenAI (Lightman et al.), repo openai/prm800k

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 2–15 on MATH-500 (500 problems; competition math elicits long chains of thought, so reasoning tokens dominate. The full 5,000-problem test set costs ~10x and is why MATH-500 exists)

human_baseline.note: The paper reports a stark human RANGE, not a point: a three-time IMO gold medalist scored 90% while a computer-science PhD student who dislikes math scored ~40%. The gauge uses the IMO-gold 90% as the reference line — the expert ceiling that reasoning models have now surpassed — and the 40% lower bound lives here. For competition math, 'human performance' is nearly meaningless without naming the human; this is the starkest range-not-a-point case on the wiki (cf. AGIEval, GPQA).

records.statistical_note: MATH-500 is 500 problems → ±~2.5pt (95% CI) near 90%. The 7 subjects × 5 difficulty levels enable fine-grained analysis, but any single level×subject cell is tiny (tens of problems) — never compare models on 'Level-5 Geometry' alone. As at the saturated frontier, aggregate gaps under a few points are noise; the bigger issue is equivalence-checker disagreement (see Scoring methodology).

contamination.mitigation: None, and compounded. Public since 2021, MIT-licensed, with full worked solutions mirrored across the web. Worse: the PRM800K release (2023) put step-level solutions to MATH TRAINING problems into wide circulation as process-supervision data — valuable for research, but more of the benchmark's solution structure in the open. MATH-500's cost motivation is partly entangled with this: it is drawn to avoid the train/PRM overlap and to make grading tractable. Fully static, no refresh. Treat near-ceiling scores as memorization-inclusive.

Timeline dates are official model launch dates; scores come from BenchmarkList's 2026-07-13 snapshot and are not claimed as launch-day evaluations.

contamination.mitigation: Expanded tests catch more overfitting, but both the inherited MBPP prompts and MBPP+ tests are public and versioned.

changelog.note: Reduced the BenchmarkList update to the user-requested top five MBPP+ models only and dated each score point by the model's official launch date; score provenance remains the 2026-07-13 BenchmarkList snapshot.

records.name: Mercury
records.short_description: Python code-synthesis benchmark that rewards both functional correctness and runtime efficiency against real solution distributions.
records.status_evidence: Mercury is a static 256-task public LeetCode-derived evaluation with no official maintained leaderboard or refreshed test set. Beyond remains useful for efficiency research, but the 2024 launch snapshot is no longer a frontier comparison.

authors.name: Mingzhe Du
authors.affiliation: Nanyang Technological University / National University of Singapore

variants.name: Pass@1
variants.description: Fraction of generated programs that pass the generated correctness tests, without runtime weighting.

human_baseline.note: No official human Beyond@1 baseline is reported. The comparison reference is a distribution of accepted human-written LeetCode solutions, not people answering the benchmark under controlled conditions.

records.statistical_note: Beyond depends on runtime percentiles and the execution environment. Compare models only under the same hardware, sandbox, test generators, timeout policy, sample count, and Mercury revision.

contamination.mitigation: The authors deduplicate collected solutions and use generated tests, but tasks derive from public LeetCode problems and the released evaluation data are static.

records.name: MGSM
records.short_description: A human-translated 250-problem GSM8K subset for comparing grade-school mathematical reasoning across ten languages.
records.status_evidence: The small, static translations are broadly supported by modern multilingual models, while large language gaps and prompt sensitivity still make MGSM useful diagnostically; newer perturbation-based successors test robustness more directly.

paper.title: Language Models are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners

variants.description: Question, exemplars, reasoning cue, and response use the target language.

variants.name: English chain of thought

run_config.shots: few-shot exemplars are the original protocol; maintained harness also supports zero-shot direct and CoT variants

human_baseline.note: No single aggregate human baseline was published; the arithmetic is grade-school level, while translation and language competence are part of the task.

records.statistical_note: Each language has only 250 paired items: near 50% accuracy the per-language 95% binomial interval is about +/-6.2 points. Cross-language errors are correlated because every language translates the same underlying problems.

contamination.mitigation: Human translation reduces exact English-string overlap but the underlying GSM8K questions, all translations, targets, and exemplars are public.

changelog.note: Initial page. Records 250 semantic items translated into ten target languages; the English file and cost count are documented separately rather than inflating dataset.size.

records.name: MME
records.short_description: Image benchmark with paired yes/no questions across 10 perception and 4 cognition subtasks.
records.status_evidence: Still widely supported as a compact diagnostic, but its small, public, static yes/no tasks provide limited frontier headroom; the same team now maintains harder MME-RealWorld and MME-CoT suites.

paper.title: MME: A Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models

records.maintainer: MME Benchmarks / Chaoyou Fu and collaborators

variants.name: Subtask score
variants.description: Accuracy plus accuracy+, ranging from 0 to 200 for each subtask.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: low to moderate; 2,374 short image-question prompts

human_baseline.note: No protocol-comparable aggregate human baseline is reported; the paired questions are manually authored and intended to be straightforward for people.

changelog.note: Initial page based on arXiv v5; classified as nearing saturation while preserving separate perception and cognition score axes.

records.name: MMLU
records.short_description: 57-subject multiple-choice exam spanning STEM, humanities, and social sciences — the defining knowledge benchmark of the 2020–2024 era.
records.status_evidence: Frontier models cluster at 86–92% since 2024; ~2–6% label errors put the effective ceiling near 90%, so top-model gaps are within noise.

paper.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding

records.maintainer: Center for AI Safety (CAIS) / Dan Hendrycks

metric.aggregation: macro average across 57 subjects (some reports use micro average over all questions — the two differ by up to ~1pt; always check which one a leaderboard uses)

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 10–40 (short prompts, single-token answers; 5-shot prompts dominate token count)

human_baseline.note: Estimated expert-level accuracy from the original paper (per-subject specialists, e.g. 87% for a professional-level test-taker on morality, ~90% averaged). Unspecialized human crowdworkers scored only 34.5%.

records.statistical_note: 14,042 questions → tight CIs (±~0.5pt at 85%), but per-subject splits are small (some subjects ~100 questions → ±~8pt); never compare models on a single subject. Label errors (~2–6%) dwarf sampling error at the frontier.

contamination.mitigation: None. Test set has been fully public on GitHub/HuggingFace since 2020 and appears verbatim in web-scale crawls; most modern pretraining corpora contain it despite decontamination attempts.

changelog.note: Initial page. Timeline ends at 2024 frontier cluster — post-2024 models rarely report MMLU as a headline number, which is itself the saturation signal.

records.name: MMLU-Pro
records.short_description: MMLU rebuilt to fix its flaws: 10 options instead of 4, trivia and label noise filtered out, and reasoning-heavy questions that reward chain-of-thought.
records.status_evidence: Frontier models cluster in the high 80s on MMLU-Pro by 2025–26 (leaderboards put the top ~89–90%), but cleaner labels and 10-option questions push the effective ceiling above MMLU's ~90%, so it still separates strong models where MMLU cannot. The 16–33 point accuracy drop it induced over MMLU is eroding; the trajectory points at saturation within a generation or two, hence nearing-saturation rather than active.

paper.title: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark

metric.aggregation: mean accuracy over 12,032 questions; also reported per-category across the 14 disciplines

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 10–40 (12,032 questions, and the standard 5-shot chain-of-thought protocol means long reasoning traces per item — several times MMLU's per-question token cost)

human_baseline.note: No measured human baseline. MMLU-Pro's difficulty was calibrated by model-side filtering (removing questions strong models found trivial and adding reasoning-heavy ones), not by testing humans — so unlike its parent MMLU (famous for its 89.8% expert baseline framing) and unlike GPQA (built around expert vs non-expert gaps), the successor here has no human reference line. A notable irony worth flagging when reading 'above/below human' claims: there is no human number to compare against.

records.statistical_note: 12,032 questions give tight aggregate CIs (±~0.6pt at 85%), and the 10-option format lowers the random-guess floor from 25% to 10%, so scores reflect knowledge more than test-taking. But per-category splits (14 disciplines) are much smaller — do not compare models on a single discipline. As frontier scores compress into the high 80s, top-model gaps under a couple of points are again approaching noise.

contamination.mitigation: Public and ungated on HuggingFace, and fully static with no refreshed variant. Contamination risk is lower than MMLU's mainly because it launched in mid-2024 — less crawl exposure so far — but it is rising, and many questions are drawn from public STEM problem sets (e.g. exam and textbook sources) that may themselves appear in training data. Treat it as medium now, trending up.

changelog.note: Initial page. Second `nearing-saturation` status on the wiki. Timeline holds the four launch-era points from the MMLU-Pro paper (GPT-4-Turbo 63.7, Claude 3 Opus 68.5, Gemini 1.5 Pro 69.0, GPT-4o 72.6), all 5-shot CoT and marked independent (the authors evaluated models they did not build); model dates are the models' real release dates, scores are the paper's. Later 2025–26 frontier scores (high 80s, leaderboards ~89–90%) are described in prose but NOT plotted: no single authoritative per-model source with a verified release date was confirmed, so points were omitted rather than fabricated (Artificial Analysis linked as the live reference). Human baseline is null by design — MMLU-Pro calibrated difficulty via model filtering, not human testing.

records.name: MMLU-Redux
records.short_description: A manual error audit of MMLU: experts re-annotated thousands of questions and found ~6.5% are broken — the evidence base for MMLU's label-noise ceiling.
records.status_evidence: As a competition benchmark, MMLU-Redux is a corrected slice of MMLU: it inherits MMLU's contamination and frontier convergence, so it does not differentiate top models — saturated by CLAUDE.md's definition (usefulness as a model-differentiating eval). Its ENDURING value is different and non-competitive: it remains an actively-used forensic reference and audit methodology for measuring label noise. Status here reflects the eval role; the still-active reference role is documented in prose. saturated_date is set to its launch — it described an already-saturated parent from birth.

paper.title: Are We Done with MMLU?

records.maintainer: Edinburgh DAWG (Gema et al.); repo/dataset edinburgh-dawg/mmlu-redux-2.0

metric.primary: accuracy on the re-annotated (error-corrected) MMLU questions (%)
metric.aggregation: accuracy over the corrected question set; the paper's core analysis compares reported-vs-corrected accuracy and how rankings shift per subject

harnesses.name: lm-evaluation-harness (standard MMLU harness on the corrected set)

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 1–5 (5,700 corrected multiple-choice items evaluated with the standard direct-answer MMLU protocol; cheap — the cost of Redux is the human annotation, not model inference)

human_baseline.note: No separate human baseline. MMLU-Redux inherits MMLU's context, where an ~89.8% expert baseline was the historical reference. Redux's contribution is orthogonal to a human score: it measures how much of MMLU's headroom was illusory (label noise), not human vs model performance. See the parent MMLU page for the baseline discussion.

records.statistical_note: The original audit re-annotated 3,000 questions across 30 subjects (14 expert annotators); the expanded Redux 2.0 covers 5,700 across all 57 subjects. Overall ~6.5% of questions contain errors, but the rate is wildly uneven — near zero in some subjects, and as high as ~57% in Virology (the original 30-subject audit already flagged it above 25%). This unevenness is the point: a benchmark's effective ceiling is set by its worst subjects, so per-subject error rates matter more than the headline average.

contamination.mitigation: Inherits MMLU's contamination completely — these ARE MMLU questions, corrected. Public since 2020 (as MMLU), fully static, ungated. Correcting the labels does nothing to reduce memorization risk; if anything the questions are more discussed now. Risk is high for the same reasons as the parent.

changelog.note: Initial page. First audit/diagnostic entry on the wiki — precedent for future error-analysis and contamination-detection suites. Performance timeline is intentionally EMPTY: MMLU-Redux is a corrected reference set and audit methodology, not a competition leaderboard, so labs do not report headline Redux scores over time — plotting a model-vs-time race would misrepresent what it is. The gauge and timeline therefore render their empty/degraded state by design (not for lack of sourcing). Human baseline null (inherits MMLU's context). Figures (~6.5% overall, Virology worst) are stated to agree exactly with the citations on the parent MMLU page; dataset.size is 5,700 (Redux 2.0, the current primary configuration) per the size-matches-primary convention, with the original 3,000/30-subject audit noted.

records.name: MMMU
records.short_description: College-level multimodal questions across 30 subjects and 183 subfields, with interleaved text and diverse images.
records.status_evidence: Still a common broad benchmark, but the maintainers introduced the harder MMMU-Pro in 2024 and released original test answers in 2026, weakening MMMU's value as a held-out frontier signal.

metric.aggregation: instance-weighted accuracy across multiple-choice and open questions after rule-based response extraction; report validation and test separately

run_config.shots: zero-shot or subject-level few-shot using the 150-example development set

records.name: MT-Bench
records.short_description: 80 curated multi-turn questions across 8 skills, each a two-turn conversation scored by a strong LLM judge on a 1–10 scale.
records.status_evidence: The 80 two-turn questions are fixed, public, and heavily exercised across research and leaderboards, so the test set is both widely memorized and increasingly saturated (top models score 8.5–9.0 on a 1–10 scale where 9 is a realistic ceiling). It remains a standard, still-discriminative LLM-judge eval, but the fixed set is the constraint: refreshed or held-out variants are the future direction.

paper.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

records.license: Apache-2.0 (FastChat tooling; question data distributed with the repo)

metric.judge_model: GPT-4 (original paper; later reported with GPT-4-family judges, so cross-time scores are comparable only when the judge is the same)
metric.aggregation: mean of a strong LLM judge's 1–10 score over the 80 two-turn questions, averaged across the two turns; also reported per category or category-grouped

variants.name: Win-rate vs baseline
variants.description: MT-Bench is also reported as a pairwise win-rate against a reference model: for each of the 80 conversations, the judge declares a winner on each turn, and the score is the fraction of turns won rather than a mean 1–10 rating. This is the reporting convention used on the original leaderboard and for many model comparisons.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 5–25 (the per-turn judge calls to a frontier model dominate; ~160 judged answers, each pass scoring a frontier model plus a judge pass)

human_baseline.note: No canonical human score on the 1–10 judge scale has been published. The paper instead validated the judge against human preference annotations: GPT-4-judge agreement with human preference exceeded 80%, roughly matching human–human agreement on the same annotations. That is an agreement check, not a human competence score.

records.statistical_note: 80 two-turn questions, with 4 or fewer per category for three of the eight categories, is small enough that reported top-model gaps of a few tenths of a point on a 1–10 scale are close to noise; treat sub-~0.3 point differences (and any single-category comparison) with caution.

contamination.mitigation: The 80 questions are fixed, shipped inside the FastChat repo, and have been used heavily across research, leaderboards, and (per several labs) included in instruction-tuning and alignment data mixtures. There is no refreshed or held-out MT-Bench; the classification question is therefore mostly fairness across contemporary models on the same fixed set.

changelog.note: Initial page. Timeline restricted to the one authoritative score cited in the original paper (GPT-4, ~8.99), because reported MT-Bench numbers vary with the judge model, judge prompt, and greedy-decoding version, and no single source tracks consistent numbers; additional points are omitted rather than fabricated.

records.name: PutnamBench
records.short_description: Formal theorem-proving on Putnam problems — models write a complete Lean/Isabelle/Coq proof, machine-checked by the proof assistant's kernel.
records.status_evidence: The wiki's first formal-proving benchmark and, for reasonable budgets, still far from solved. Through most of 2024–2025 the best systems solved single digits of the Lean set (Goedel-Prover 7 at pass@512; GPT-4o ~1). General reasoning models at pass@1 remain low (GPT-5 ReAct ~28–42 of ~660, single digits %). Heavy-compute systems have since climbed steeply — ByteDance's Seed-Prover reportedly ~581/672 Lean at ~10 GPU-days per problem, and in Jan 2026 Logical Intelligence's Aleph CLAIMED 668/672 (99.4%, agentic pass@1) topping the board — but these use enormous or single-source, unreproduced budgets, and the Isabelle/Coq subsets and the harder 'no-answer' variant remain far less attacked. What would move this to nearing-saturation: independent reproduction of high solve rates across languages under disclosed, comparable budgets.

paper.title: PutnamBench: Evaluating Neural Theorem-Provers on the Putnam Mathematical Competition
paper.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks (ICML 2024 AI4Math Best Paper)

records.maintainer: George Tsoukalas et al. (UT Austin); repo trishullab/PutnamBench (canonical — leaderboard + results.json)
records.license: Apache-2.0 (Lean 4, Isabelle), MIT (Coq); informal problem statements included with MAA permission

metric.primary: problems with a complete, kernel-verified formal proof — Lean subset (count / 672)
metric.aggregation: count of problems for which a proof-assistant-verified proof was found, reported PER LANGUAGE (Lean 672 / Isabelle 640 / Coq 412) and per variant (answer-in-statement vs no-answer). Never blended into one number

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: Enormously variable and the whole story: from a general model at pass@1 (cheap, low solve rate) to fine-tuned provers at pass@512 to special systems at ~10 GPU-days PER PROBLEM (ByteDance) to agentic runs at ~$68 average / $1400 cap per problem (Aleph). A 'solved N' figure is meaningless without this budget

human_baseline.note: No usable human baseline, and the mismatch is starker than anywhere else on the wiki. The Putnam is famously brutal: the median score among the elite students who sit it is often 0 or 1 out of 120 (in 2024, ~40% of ~4,000 entrants scored 0–1; only 5 perfect scores in 85 years). But humans solve Putnam INFORMALLY, under a 6-hour limit, with no machine — while PutnamBench requires a COMPLETE FORMAL proof, with no time limit and a proof assistant. Humans and machines are not doing the same task, so a direct baseline comparison is more strained here than for any answer-based benchmark (cf. AIME's 'low even for excellent humans' point, taken further). Hence null, not a number.

records.statistical_note: Scores are per-language and per-variant, and the totals grow as new Putnam years are formalized (a living benchmark — see Task details), so cite the denominator and 'as of' date. The dominant confound is NOT sampling noise but COMPUTE/SAMPLING BUDGET: results span pass@10 to pass@512-and-beyond, plus GPU-days-per-problem agentic runs, and these differ by tens of percentage points on the same benchmark. A special-purpose system at pass@512 and a general model at pass@1 solving similar counts are very different achievements. The leaderboard itself notes it is seeking a better way to indicate differing budgets.

contamination.mitigation: A genuinely different contamination profile from every answer-based maths page. The formalizations are hand-crafted (not scraped text), and the formal PROOFS are not published as a solution set the way GSM8K/MATH worked solutions are — so the usual leakage vector is weaker. Crucially, the formal-proof requirement makes memorization far less useful: you cannot shortcut a kernel-checked Lean proof by recalling a number or a memorized informal argument. Working the other way: the Putnam problem STATEMENTS are public and decades of informal solutions circulate widely, which can leak proof strategies. Net: medium, effectively toward the low end — lower than any answer-based maths benchmark here, but not FrontierMath-low, because the statements are so public.

changelog.note: Initial page. Fifth `maths` benchmark and the wiki's FIRST formal theorem-proving benchmark — a distinct sub-area (formal methods) that grades a machine-checked proof, not a final answer. Firsts: split license (Apache-2.0 Lean/Isabelle, MIT Coq); `scoring: unit-tests` used as the closest existing value for proof-assistant kernel verification (a dedicated `formal-verification` value is flagged as warranted — miniF2F/ProofNet will re-raise it). Totals are 'as of 2026-07-22': 1,724 formalizations (672 Lean 4 / 640 Isabelle / 412 Coq), Putnam 1962–2025 — a LIVING benchmark grown from the paper's ~640 theorems / ~1,697 formalizations. size=672 (Lean, the primary reported/leaderboard config). Timeline plots only comparable/general-budget Lean points (GPT-4o ~0.2%, Goedel-Prover 1.1% pass@512, GPT-5 6.4% pass@1); ByteDance Seed-Prover (~581/672, ~10 GPU-days/problem, independent) and Aleph (668/672 = 99.4%, Jan 2026, single-source Logical Intelligence, agentic pass@1) are in status_evidence/Known issues but NOT plotted, to avoid smoothing enormous- or single-source-budget results into a saturation trend. Aleph framed as a claimed recent frontier result pending independent reproduction — its 15 counterexample fixes to malformed formalizations WERE verified by the PutnamBench team. SCHEMA FLAGS in summary: formal-verification scoring value; a formal-methods grouping mechanism (tags/secondary-capability); pass_at can't hold the budget range; structured per-point run-config (5th case).
