records.name: SimpleQA
records.short_description: 4,326 short fact-seeking questions chosen to stump GPT-4 — a hallucination test graded correct / incorrect / not-attempted.
records.status_evidence: Still discriminating hard. Frontier models remain well short of the ceiling on parametric recall: GPT-4o 38% correct at launch, GPT-4.5 ~62% by early 2025 — climbing but nowhere near solved, and reasoning-tuned models do not automatically help (o1-mini scored 8%). What would move it off 'active': frontier 'correct' crossing ~85–90% (approaching the label ceiling), OR retrieval-augmented deployment becoming universal enough that closed-book parametric recall stops mattering. Neither has happened.

paper.title: Measuring Short-Form Factuality in Large Language Models

metric.judge_model: Prompted ChatGPT classifier that compares the predicted answer to the reference (GPT-4o in OpenAI's reference implementation, simple-evals). Scores graded by different grader models or prompt versions are not strictly comparable.
metric.aggregation: each answer classified correct / incorrect / not-attempted, then aggregated over 4,326 questions

variants.name: correct given attempted
variants.description: Accuracy among only the questions the model actually attempted (correct / (correct + incorrect)). Rewards a model for answering when right; unaffected by declining. High here + low 'correct' = a cautious model that knows little but rarely bluffs.

variants.name: F-score
variants.description: Harmonic mean of 'correct' and 'correct given attempted', equal to 2c/(2c+2i+n) for correct c, incorrect i, not-attempted n. The single number that rewards knowing answers AND declining when unsure — the paper's summary metric and the one SimpleQA Verified reports as F1.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 3–15 (4,326 short questions; answers are brief, but every one needs a separate LLM-grader call, so the grader roughly doubles the API cost)

human_baseline.note: No human baseline — and arguably none is meaningful. The questions were deliberately selected to be obscure (adversarially filtered so frontier models got them wrong), so a human sitting the test closed-book would mostly measure luck, and open-book would measure Googling, not knowledge. The paper reports a 94.4% agreement rate from a third annotator, but that measures dataset quality (are the answers indisputable?), not human question-answering ability. This is the first benchmark on the wiki where a human reference line is not just missing but conceptually beside the point.

records.statistical_note: 4,326 questions give a reasonably tight aggregate CI (±~1.5pt at 40% correct). The more important caveats are non-sampling: the LLM grader introduces its own error and version drift (see Known issues), and because SimpleQA reports three outcomes, a single 'accuracy' number hides whether a model is knowledgeable or merely bold — always read 'correct' alongside 'not attempted'.

contamination.mitigation: Public and ungated (openai/simple-evals), fully static, no refresh cycle. The irony is acute: a benchmark built to measure hallucination can itself be memorized. It was adversarially collected against 2024-era models, so the exact Q&A pairs — now discussed in papers, blog posts, and leaderboards — increasingly enter post-2024 training corpora, and a model can 'improve' by having seen the answer key rather than by knowing more. SimpleQA Verified (2025) partly re-collects and cleans to push back on this.

changelog.note: Initial page. First `active`-status benchmark on the wiki (completing the four-status taxonomy), first `llm-judge` PRIMARY scoring with a real judge_model value, and first entry with a genuinely-null (not just missing) human baseline. Timeline is on the 'correct' axis: four launch-paper points (Claude 3 Opus 23.5 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 28.9 marked independent — OpenAI is not their vendor; GPT-4o 38.2 and o1-preview 42.7 marked vendor-reported) plus GPT-4.5 62.5 (2025-02-27, vendor-reported, GPT-4.5 launch). The four launch-paper models predate the benchmark, so their scores are dated to SimpleQA's launch (2024-11-07) — when the scores were actually established — rather than to each model's release, which would place them before launch and clamp them to the axis origin. Scores are still CLIMBING toward an unknown ceiling — no plateau to draw. 2025–26 numbers beyond GPT-4.5 exist but were left to prose where a single authoritative per-model source wasn't confirmed. SimpleQA Verified (Google DeepMind, arXiv:2509.07968) and Chinese SimpleQA (Alibaba, arXiv:2411.07140) added to lineage.variants (pages not written; slugs won't resolve yet).

authors.name: Yue Wang
authors.affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

metric.judge_model: GPT-4o (the paper's automated evaluator — see scoring methodology for the reproducibility caveat)
metric.aggregation: weighted mean over constraints: WCSR = Σ w_j·s_j / Σ w_j, where s_j ∈ {0,1} per constraint, with structural constraints weighted w_s = 2 and intra-turn constraints w_r = 1

variants.name: CSR — Constraint Satisfaction Rate
variants.description: Unweighted average proportion of satisfied constraints across all instructions, treating every constraint equally.

variants.name: ISR — Instruction Satisfaction Rate
variants.description: Binary per instruction: 1 only when every constraint in that instruction was satisfied.

variants.name: DRFR — Decomposed Requirement Following Rate
variants.description: Global requirement-following ratio: satisfied scoring questions summed over all instructions, divided by the total number of scoring questions.

human_baseline.note: No protocol-comparable human baseline published. The 'Golden Context' setup drops each model into the same curated dialogue history rather than one it generated, but the paper reports no human agreement with the GPT-4o judge on model outputs.

records.statistical_note: 155 dialogues and a per-constraint score grid under a single LLM judge; per-turn and per-relationship cells are small. Treat WCSR gaps under a few points as noise until a leaderboard reports confidence intervals or a second judge.

contamination.mitigation: The dataset was released on 2025-02-20 and postdates most 2024 training cutoffs, so direct memorization is currently less of a risk. The structural relationships are a behavioral/semantic target rather than a fixed factual test set, so memorizing one dialogue does little to help on unseen dialogue flows.

records.name: TruthfulQA
records.short_description: 817 adversarial questions probing whether models repeat common human misconceptions — famous for finding that bigger models were often less truthful.
records.status_evidence: By 2023 post-RLHF models exceeded the 94% human truthfulness baseline — but largely because the exact misconceptions TruthfulQA targets are what alignment tuning trains against, and the dataset itself leaked into alignment mixes. Saturation here reflects targeted contamination, not broadly truthful models. saturated_date (2023-06) marks the ChatGPT/GPT-4 era when the inverse-scaling trend reversed.

paper.title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods

metric.primary: MC2 (normalized probability mass on true answers, %)
metric.aggregation: mean over 817 questions (no category weighting)

variants.name: MC1
variants.description: Single-true multiple choice: accuracy at assigning the highest probability to the one correct answer among 4–5 options.

variants.name: MC2
variants.description: Multi-true multiple choice: the normalized total probability the model places on the set of true answers. The most-reported number, and the site's headline metric.

variants.name: generation (truthful %)
variants.description: Open-ended answer graded for truthfulness (and separately informativeness). The task with a human baseline, and the axis the timeline uses.
variants.judge_model: GPT-judge — a fine-tuned GPT-3 curie, now deprecated; commonly replaced by GPT-4-as-judge, which makes cross-year generation scores non-comparable.

cost_estimate.approx_usd_frontier_model: 1–5 (817 short items; MC1/MC2 need only log-probs. The generation task adds a GPT-4-judge pass, which costs more)

human_baseline.note: 94% truthful on the generation task in the original paper (human validators). No published human baseline exists for the MC1/MC2 multiple-choice variants, so the timeline and gauge track generation truthfulness to stay comparable to this number.

records.statistical_note: 817 questions → roughly ±3pt across the 60–90% range (95% CI). The 38 category splits (some <20 questions) are far too small for per-category comparison. Metric choice (MC1 vs MC2 vs generation) moves scores more than most model-to-model gaps do.

contamination.mitigation: None, and uniquely self-defeating: the misconceptions TruthfulQA targets are exactly what RLHF and Constitutional-style alignment tuning is trained to avoid, and the dataset itself appears in some alignment/instruction mixes. Modern scores partly measure exposure to the benchmark's own patterns.

changelog.note: Updated dataset URL to the domenicrosati/TruthfulQA HuggingFace mirror.

records.name: WinoGrande
records.short_description: Binary fill-in-the-blank commonsense problems, scaled from Winograd schemas and adversarially filtered to reduce dataset shortcuts.
records.status_evidence: The original XL result was 79.1% against a 94.0% human estimate, leaving real headroom, but the static public inputs and widespread validation-set use make modern scores contamination-sensitive.

paper.title: WinoGrande: An Adversarial Winograd Schema Challenge at Scale

metric.aggregation: Mean correctness over examples; each prediction is option 1 or option 2, so random chance is 50%. Official test labels are hidden and evaluated by submission.

variants.name: lm-eval likelihood-ranked accuracy
variants.description: Ranks the two candidate substitutions by conditional log-likelihood on the public 1,267-example validation split; this is not the hidden-label official test protocol.

run_config.shots: zero-shot by default in lm-evaluation-harness; original paper fine-tunes on XS/S/M/L/XL training subsets

human_baseline.note: Crowd-worker estimate reported by the original paper; compare with care because current lm-eval runs use the validation split rather than the hidden-label official test set.

records.statistical_note: On the 1,267-example validation split, a 50% accuracy estimate has an approximate 95% binomial margin of error of +/-2.8 points; paired predictions are preferable for close model comparisons.

contamination.mitigation: Official test labels remain hidden, and lm-evaluation-harness exposes a decontamination query, but the test inputs and the fully labeled validation split are public and unchanged.

changelog.note: Added performance timeline with fine-tuned and few-shot scores from BERT-Large, RoBERTa, GPT-3, PaLM, GPT-4, Llama 2/3, and Claude 3 Opus. Model names include protocol notes (fine-tuned vs few-shot) because protocol differences dominate comparability.
